## What you'll learn

- Why the share of the transcriptome isn't the share of the community.
- How to check that each strain has enough inserts to analyse.
- How to normalise counts for exploration (TPM, CLR), and check replicates with PCA and correlations.
- How to read a strain's growth state from its ribosomal protein transcripts.

::: {.lesson-meta}
<span><span aria-hidden="true">⏱</span> **About 45 min**</span>
<span><span aria-hidden="true">💻</span> **Runs in this page:** R in your browser, nothing to install</span>
<span><span aria-hidden="true">📦</span> **Data:** Oligo-MM12 mice, LPS vs PBS</span>
:::

## The data

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `samples.csv` | One row per mouse: sample ID and treatment (LPS or PBS) |
| `genes.csv.gz` | One row per gene: locus tag, strain (`genome`), length, KEGG ortholog (KO) and KEGG pathways |
| `counts.csv.gz` | Inserts per gene (rows) in each sample (columns), as produced in Part 1 |
| `kegg_ko.csv` | Names of the KEGG orthologs |

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())

samples <- read_csv("data/samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
genes <- read_csv("data/genes.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
counts <- read_csv("data/counts.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)
kegg_ko <- read_csv("data/kegg_ko.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# one row per gene per sample, with the gene's strain and length
counts_long <- counts %>%
  pivot_longer(-locus_tag, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") %>%
  left_join(select(genes, locus_tag, genome, length), by = "locus_tag") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id")

strain_colours <- c(
  YL32 = "#149AB3", KB18 = "#616161", I48 = "#C26215", YL27 = "#F59C46",
  YL45 = "#E30C4B", I46 = "#2C5D52", YL58 = "#163A1A", YL31 = "#099334",
  YL2 = "#282E68", I49 = "#3DB077", YL44 = "#AC7FB6", KB1 = "#42AB34"
)
cat("Loaded", nrow(genes), "genes from", n_distinct(genes$genome), "strains and",
    nrow(samples), "samples.\n")
cat("Ready: packages and data are loaded.\n")
```

Have a look at the tables:

```{webr}
samples
genes
counts
```

How many genes have a KO, i.e. a known function? Count them overall and per strain:

```{webr}
genes %>%
  summarise(genes = n(), with_KO = sum(!is.na(KO)), share = mean(!is.na(KO)))

genes %>%
  group_by(genome) %>%
  summarise(genes = n(), with_KO = sum(!is.na(KO)), share = mean(!is.na(KO))) %>%
  arrange(share)
```

Only 46% of the genes have a KO, and this varies between strains, from 36% in I46 to 63% in I49. The rest have no known function, which will matter in Part 4.

## Step 1: who dominates the transcriptome?

Sum the counts of each strain's genes in each sample, and divide by the sample's total:

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
strain_inserts <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(sample_id, Treatment, genome) %>%
  summarise(inserts = sum(count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  mutate(share = inserts / sum(inserts)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(strain_inserts, aes(sample_id, share, fill = genome)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_grid(~ Treatment, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = strain_colours) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of transcripts", fill = "Strain") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```

Three strains, YL32, I48 and YL58, make up about 70% of all transcripts. Some strains barely appear, and YL2 is absent.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("YL32 makes up 38% of the transcripts in PBS mice. Does that mean 38% of the bacterial cells are YL32?", [
  {text: "Yes, every cell contributes transcripts", correct: false, why: "Cells differ in how much mRNA they make: fast-growing cells make far more than dormant ones."},
  {text: "No: the transcript share depends on abundance and on activity", correct: true, why: "Transcripts = gene copies × expression. To measure composition, use DNA (metagenomics, 16S) instead."},
  {text: "No, because YL32 has the largest genome", correct: false, why: "Genome size plays a part, but even strains with equal genomes can differ widely in mRNA per cell."}
])
```

To estimate composition, use DNA: 16S rRNA gene sequencing or a metagenome. Marker-gene profilers such as [mOTUs](https://motu-tool.org/) can also be run on the metatranscriptome itself, since they rely on genes that every cell expresses.

## Step 2: is there enough data for each strain?

A sample with 10 million inserts might have 8 million from one strain and only 50,000 from another. Analyses are done **strain by strain**, so what matters is each strain's depth. In this lesson, we ask for **at least 500,000 inserts per strain per sample**.

### Exercise: which strains can we analyse?

Count, for each strain and treatment, the samples with at least 500,000 inserts.

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
#| exercise: ex_depth
depth <- strain_inserts %>%
  group_by(genome, Treatment) %>%
  summarise(n_adequate = sum(______), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(depth, aes(Treatment, genome, fill = n_adequate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n_adequate)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "steelblue", limits = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Samples with\n≥ 500k inserts")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_depth"}
`sum()` of a logical vector counts the `TRUE` values. Compare each sample's `inserts` with `5e5`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_depth"}
```r
depth <- strain_inserts %>%
  group_by(genome, Treatment) %>%
  summarise(n_adequate = sum(inserts >= 5e5), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(depth, aes(Treatment, genome, fill = n_adequate)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n_adequate)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "steelblue", limits = c(0, 6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Samples with\n≥ 500k inserts")
```
Only I48 and YL32 have enough inserts in all 12 samples. YL58 has enough in 8.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_depth
#| check: true
expected <- strain_inserts %>%
  group_by(genome, Treatment) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(inserts >= 5e5), .groups = "drop")
ok <- is.data.frame(depth) && "n_adequate" %in% names(depth) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    arrange(depth, genome, Treatment)$n_adequate,
    arrange(expected, genome, Treatment)$n
  ))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Right. Only I48 and YL32 are deep enough in every sample; we'll focus on them and YL58.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: n_adequate should count samples with inserts >= 5e5.")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## What about the rare strains?
With few inserts, most genes have counts of 0 or 1, and nothing can be tested reliably. You can still describe them, but leave them out of differential expression, or sequence deeper.
:::

## Step 3: normalising for exploration

Raw counts can't be compared directly:

1. **Gene length:** longer genes collect more inserts at the same expression.
2. **Depth:** each strain has a different number of inserts in each sample.
3. **Compositionality:** counts are only meaningful relative to the other genes in the sample.

For plots and PCA, we normalise **within each strain**: then a strain's depth or abundance doesn't matter, only the relative expression of its genes. (Differential expression in Part 3 uses its own normalisation.)

### TPM: transcripts per million

1. Divide each gene's count by its length in kilobases: reads per kilobase (RPK).
2. Divide by the sum of RPK over all of the strain's genes in that sample, and multiply by a million.

The TPM values of a strain then add up to one million in every sample.

### Exercise: write a TPM function

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tpm
calculate_tpm <- function(counts, lengths) {
  rpk <- ______
  rpk / sum(rpk) * 1e6
}

calculate_tpm(c(10, 20), c(1000, 2000))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_tpm"}
Reads per kilobase is `counts` divided by the length in kilobases, `lengths / 1000`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_tpm"}
```r
calculate_tpm <- function(counts, lengths) {
  rpk <- counts / (lengths / 1000)
  rpk / sum(rpk) * 1e6
}

calculate_tpm(c(10, 20), c(1000, 2000))
```
Both genes have 10 reads per kilobase, so they get the same TPM: half a million each.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tpm
#| check: true
ok <- is.function(calculate_tpm) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(calculate_tpm(c(10, 20), c(1000, 2000)), c(5e5, 5e5))) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(calculate_tpm(c(5, 0, 30), c(500, 900, 3000)), c(5e5, 0, 5e5)))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct: equal reads per kilobase give equal TPM.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: calculate_tpm(c(10, 20), c(1000, 2000)) should give 500000 for both genes.")
}
```

Now apply it to every strain in every sample:

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
calculate_tpm <- function(counts, lengths) {
  rpk <- counts / (lengths / 1000)
  rpk / sum(rpk) * 1e6
}

expr <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(genome, sample_id) %>%
  mutate(tpm = calculate_tpm(count, length)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Each strain's TPM adds up to a million in every sample
expr %>%
  group_by(genome, sample_id) %>%
  summarise(total_tpm = sum(tpm), .groups = "drop") %>%
  head()
```

### Log and CLR transformations

Expression values span several orders of magnitude, so we look at them on a log scale. Two common choices:

- **log2(TPM + 0.5):** the pseudocount 0.5 avoids taking the log of zero.
- **CLR (centred log-ratio):** each gene's log value minus the mean log value of all of the strain's genes in that sample. It's made for compositional data: it compares each gene to the strain's "average gene".

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
expr <- expr %>%
  group_by(genome, sample_id) %>%
  mutate(
    log2_tpm = log2(tpm + 0.5),
    clr = log(tpm + 0.5) - mean(log(tpm + 0.5))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

expr %>%
  filter(genome == "I48", sample_id == "AU647") %>%
  pivot_longer(c(tpm, log2_tpm, clr), names_to = "scale") %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("tpm", "log2_tpm", "clr"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "I48 in one sample: the same genes on three scales", x = NULL, y = "Genes")
```

TPM is dominated by a few very highly expressed genes. On the log and CLR scales you can see the whole distribution, with a spike of unexpressed genes on the left. CLR is the log scale shifted so that each sample is centred on zero.

## Step 4: do replicates agree?

### PCA within one strain

PCA summarises each sample's expression profile, over many genes, in a few axes. Samples with similar profiles end up close together. Change `strain` and rerun to look at other strains.

We don't use all genes:

1. **Drop genes that are barely detected.** A gene with almost no inserts tells us nothing about expression, only about chance and depth. We keep genes with at least 10 inserts in at least 6 samples (the size of one treatment group, so genes expressed in only one treatment are kept).
2. **Keep the 500 most variable genes.** Genes whose expression barely changes between samples add noise but no information about how samples differ. This is also the default of `plotPCA()` in DESeq2.

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
strain <- "I48"

# genes with at least 10 inserts in at least 6 samples
detected <- counts_long %>%
  filter(genome == strain) %>%
  group_by(locus_tag) %>%
  summarise(n_samples = sum(count >= 10)) %>%
  filter(n_samples >= 6) %>%
  pull(locus_tag)

clr_matrix <- expr %>%
  filter(genome == strain, locus_tag %in% detected) %>%
  select(sample_id, locus_tag, clr) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = locus_tag, values_from = clr) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("sample_id") %>%
  as.matrix()

# the 500 genes whose CLR values vary most between samples
top_genes <- names(sort(apply(clr_matrix, 2, var), decreasing = TRUE))[1:500]

cat(length(detected), "of", n_distinct(expr$locus_tag[expr$genome == strain]),
    strain, "genes are detected; the PCA uses the 500 most variable.\n")

pca <- prcomp(clr_matrix[, top_genes])
explained <- round(100 * summary(pca)$importance[2, 1:2])

as.data.frame(pca$x) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("sample_id") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  ggplot(aes(PC1, PC2, colour = Treatment, label = sample_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = paste("PCA of", strain, "gene expression (CLR)"),
       x = paste0("PC1 (", explained[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", explained[2], "%)"))
```

In I48, the first axis largely separates LPS from PBS mice. But four mice sit in between: two LPS (AU657, AU658) and two PBS (AU648, AU649). Is treatment the only thing the first axis captures?

### Exercise: what else drives the first axis?

The samples were sequenced to very different depths. Compute the total number of inserts in each sample, and plot it against the first axis.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pca_depth
sample_depth <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  summarise(depth = ______)

as.data.frame(pca$x) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("sample_id") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  left_join(sample_depth, by = "sample_id") %>%
  ggplot(aes(depth / 1e6, PC1, colour = Treatment, label = sample_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Inserts in the sample (millions, log scale)", title = paste(strain, ": first axis against depth"))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_pca_depth"}
The depth of a sample is the sum of the counts of all genes in it: `sum(count)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_pca_depth"}
```r
sample_depth <- counts_long %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  summarise(depth = sum(count))

as.data.frame(pca$x) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("sample_id") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample_id") %>%
  left_join(sample_depth, by = "sample_id") %>%
  ggplot(aes(depth / 1e6, PC1, colour = Treatment, label = sample_id)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Inserts in the sample (millions, log scale)", title = paste(strain, ": first axis against depth"))
```
The samples fall into two groups: 3–6 million and 12–18 million inserts. The first axis follows depth closely, and the four "in-between" mice are exactly those whose depth is unusual for their treatment: AU657 and AU658 are deeply sequenced LPS mice, AU648 and AU649 shallow PBS mice.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pca_depth
#| check: true
expected <- colSums(as.matrix(counts[, -1]))
ok <- is.data.frame(sample_depth) && "depth" %in% names(sample_depth) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(sample_depth$depth[match(names(expected), sample_depth$sample_id)],
                   unname(expected)))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct. The first axis mixes treatment with sequencing depth.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: depth should be the sum of all counts in each sample.")
}
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Treatment and depth are partly confounded
Four of the six LPS mice were sequenced shallowly, and four of the six PBS mice deeply. In shallow samples, more genes have zero or very few counts, which changes their profiles. So the first axis mixes the effect of LPS with the effect of depth, and you can't fully separate the two in this dataset. In your own experiments, **randomise samples across sequencing runs and depths**, so that technical differences can't line up with your groups. Try `"YL32"`, `"YL58"` and `"KB18"` too: the treatments separate less cleanly there.
:::

### Sample correlations

A correlation heatmap shows the same thing differently: every pair of samples, and how similar their profiles are.

```{webr}
cor_matrix <- cor(t(clr_matrix), method = "spearman")
ord <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cor_matrix))$order
sample_order <- rownames(cor_matrix)[ord]

as.data.frame(cor_matrix) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("sample_1") %>%
  pivot_longer(-sample_1, names_to = "sample_2", values_to = "rho") %>%
  mutate(sample_1 = factor(sample_1, sample_order), sample_2 = factor(sample_2, sample_order)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample_1, sample_2, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rho)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = paste(strain, ": sample-to-sample correlation"), x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```

Samples are ordered by hierarchical clustering. Replicates should correlate highly; a sample that correlates poorly with all others is a candidate outlier (e.g. a failed library).

## Step 5: how fast are the strains growing?

A growing cell needs many ribosomes, so it spends a large share of its transcription on **ribosomal proteins**. The share of a strain's transcripts that encode ribosomal proteins is a rough proxy for its growth rate. Because it's a share *within* the strain, the strain's abundance cancels out: more cells mean more ribosomal *and* more other transcripts. Compare it between samples of one strain, not between strains: their baselines differ (about 0.2–0.5% in YL32, 3–4% in I48).

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
ribosomal_kos <- kegg_ko %>%
  filter(grepl("subunit ribosomal protein", name)) %>%
  pull(KO)

# some genes have several KOs, separated by commas
genes <- genes %>%
  mutate(is_ribosomal = vapply(strsplit(coalesce(KO, ""), ","),
                               function(k) any(k %in% ribosomal_kos), logical(1)))

counts_ribo <- counts_long %>%
  left_join(select(genes, locus_tag, is_ribosomal), by = "locus_tag")

cat(length(ribosomal_kos), "ribosomal protein KOs;",
    sum(genes$is_ribosomal), "ribosomal protein genes in the community\n")
```

### Exercise: ribosomal protein share

For each strain in each sample, compute the share of transcripts from ribosomal protein genes. Plot it for the three main strains.

```{webr}
#| tldr: true
#| exercise: ex_ribo
ribo <- counts_ribo %>%
  filter(genome %in% c("I48", "YL32", "YL58")) %>%
  group_by(genome, sample_id, Treatment) %>%
  summarise(ribosomal_share = ______, .groups = "drop")

ggplot(ribo, aes(Treatment, ribosomal_share, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ genome, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(y = "Transcripts from ribosomal proteins", x = NULL)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_ribo"}
Sum the counts of the ribosomal protein genes only, `sum(count[is_ribosomal])`, and divide by the sum of all counts.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_ribo"}
```r
ribo <- counts_ribo %>%
  filter(genome %in% c("I48", "YL32", "YL58")) %>%
  group_by(genome, sample_id, Treatment) %>%
  summarise(ribosomal_share = sum(count[is_ribosomal]) / sum(count), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(ribo, aes(Treatment, ribosomal_share, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ genome, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(y = "Transcripts from ribosomal proteins", x = NULL)
```
The ribosomal protein share is lower in LPS mice in all three strains, consistent with slower growth when the host is inflamed (another possibility: a sick host eats less, changing what the bacteria can feed on). The difference is clear for YL32 and YL58 (Wilcoxon p ≈ 0.002), and a trend for I48 (p ≈ 0.09). Test it with `wilcox.test(ribosomal_share ~ Treatment, data = filter(ribo, genome == "YL32"))`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_ribo
#| check: true
expected <- counts_ribo %>%
  filter(genome == "I48") %>%
  group_by(sample_id) %>%
  summarise(share = sum(count[is_ribosomal]) / sum(count))
mine <- if (is.data.frame(ribo) && "ribosomal_share" %in% names(ribo)) {
  ribo %>% filter(genome == "I48") %>% arrange(sample_id)
}
ok <- !is.null(mine) && nrow(mine) == 12 &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(mine$ribosomal_share, arrange(expected, sample_id)$share))
if (ok) {
  list(correct = TRUE, type = "success",
       message = "Correct. Ribosomal protein transcripts are lower in LPS mice, most clearly in YL32 and YL58.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, type = "error",
       message = "Not yet: divide the counts of ribosomal protein genes by all counts of the strain in that sample.")
}
```

## Check yourself

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz("Strain X has 1 million inserts in some samples and 3 million in others. Why do we normalise within each strain before PCA?", [
  {text: "So that the PCA shows differences in gene expression, not in how many inserts the strain got", correct: true, why: "Within-strain normalisation removes the strain's depth and abundance, leaving the relative expression of its genes."},
  {text: "Because PCA can't handle large numbers", correct: false, why: "PCA works with any numbers; the issue is what the differences mean."},
  {text: "To remove rare genes", correct: false, why: "Normalisation doesn't remove genes; filtering does."}
])
```

## Key points

- **Transcript share ≠ community composition:** it mixes abundance with activity.
- **Check depth per strain,** not per sample. Analyse only strains with enough inserts.
- **Normalise within each strain** for exploration: TPM, then log or CLR.
- **PCA and correlation heatmaps** show whether replicates agree and what drives the variation. Here: treatment.
- **Ribosomal protein share** is a simple proxy for growth. In LPS mice it is lower, consistent with slower growth.
